system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

data.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning. The hazard (dust and sand from fresh to strong northwesterly winds), the visibility figure (under 2,000 metres), the areas (coastal and inland), the end time (19:00, 4 March), the source, the flash-flood sentence, the protective action (take extra care when driving on open roads) and the URL all carry over without change. However, the Arabic was produced by machine translation. A named person who reads Arabic must confirm it before the alert is sent, and I cannot give that approval. A separate point: the English itself contains a flash-flood sentence that does not fit this dust alert and gives no matching protective action. The Arabic reproduces that sentence faithfully. It is outside my mandate and is recorded under no_basis.

objections.issue: The Arabic text was produced by machine translation and has not yet been confirmed by a human reviewer who reads Arabic. The guidance shown says machine-translated alert text risks material inaccuracies and needs human review. My comparison found no difference in meaning, but it does not replace sign-off by a named Arabic reader.
objections.fix: Before release, a named Arabic-reading reviewer at the issuing authority must confirm the Arabic headline, description and instruction. If the alert is issued before that review, mark the Arabic as automated translation and send an update once a human has reviewed it.

evidence.quote: relying on software to translate WEAs without review by a human translator may cause material inaccuracies in critically important alerts.
free form text content that has been subsequently reviewed by a human for correct translation, replacing automated translated content

no_basis.concern: The English description ends with 'Flash flooding is expected in low-lying areas.' This does not fit a dust and low-visibility alert, and the instruction gives no protective action for flooding. The Arabic translates the sentence accurately, so there is no translation difference. The content issue in the source should be checked by the drafter or approver.
no_basis.searched_for: Clauses on internal consistency of hazard description versus protective action within a single-language alert; none in my mandate covers source-text content errors.
